idea.why: The decomposition matches the brief's own seams: two independent streams each fetched, batched and analysed by a specialist, rejoined once, then a third agent that only does presentation. Triage logic in one prompt, day-plan logic in another, layout in a third, and no concern spread across three nodes.

structure.why: Mostly correct purpose-built types and a proportionate count. The weak point is the composer: a model freehanding a complete document every morning is a generative node doing what a deterministic template does faster, cheaper and identically each day. The Merge is near-decorative since the composer reads by node reference.

connections.why: The wiring expresses the real dependency graph almost exactly: fan-out rather than chaining, each stream chaining its genuinely dependent steps, rejoining at a two-input Merge precisely where the composer needs both. Each parser attaches to its own agent only.

answer.why: End to end it delivers, and empty-state behaviour is specified in both prompts so a quiet day produces a sane briefing. Two things a reader would notice: the dashboard is regenerated from scratch each morning so its layout cannot be relied on to look the same twice, and it arrives as mail rather than a page one opens.

appraisal: A clean, well-reasoned build: fan-out to two independent fetches, each stream aggregated and handed to a specialist with a schema-pinned output, rejoining at a Merge before a presentation-only composer. Details that matter in practice are handled, including a single shared model, defensive options on both fetches, explicit empty-day instructions, and a sticky note naming the manual setup steps. What it gets wrong is the last hop: rendering with a model makes the daily deliverable non-deterministic, slow and expensive, and the Merge it depends on carries no data. A knowledgeable user would replace the composer with a deterministic template fed by the two payloads, keeping the analysts as the genuinely model-shaped work.
